scenario: AITA For going on my best friend's dream trip and not inviting her? | Me and Mandy have been best friends since basically kindergarten, and almost since then she's been fascinated with Turkey, Croatia, and the Balkans/Mediterranean region in general. I started dating a guy from a Balkan country and was making plans to go visit him and his family, and while doing so I found this AMAZING package deal that lets you travel the Balkans, Spain, Greece, Turkey and Morocco. Seriously, it was like a once in a lifetime deal and though it's pretty expensive, it's WAY cheaper than it would be to find places to stay and travel to those places on your own. I KNEW Mandy couldn't afford it, and I KNEW it would hurt her deeply that she wasn't getting a chance to go. This trip is literally what she dreams of doing, and with me in particular, but she's been in a lot of financial trouble lately. So I told her I was planning a trip, but not any of the details. I also told another very close friend about the trip, and she looked up the same deal and decided she wanted to go as well. I said I'd love to have the company, so she bought her tickets and she's coming along too. I realized that if Mandy heard about this or found out about this before I got a chance to tell her she'd be super hurt, so I told her about the trip. She was SOOOOOOO upset. She asked about why I didn't invite her, and I told her it was because I knew she couldn't afford it and I thought it would just be salt in the wound. (I also privately think she would have made some very questionable decisions in order to fund the trip, or would have gone and then not had enough for money, or her bills, or things like that at home.) That just made it worse, and she cried, and cried about how we always said we'd go and experience those places together, and that I don't even have any interest in the region, which is pretty much true since I want to travel around Asia. I told her we could still go that in the future, and we could even do this trip in the future, but she was too hurt to want to hear that. My boyfriend thinks I am being kind of a dick, and says for his best friend, he'd have offered to pay for part to help if he could, and I guess I \*could\* but not super comfortably and idk when she'd pay me back. He also thinks she'd have been less hurt if I brought it up while I was thinking about it. My other friend agrees that it was a good idea to wait to tell her since she agrees Mandy probably would have done ANYTHING to go on that trip.

Christmas and Easter are the two biggest points of my year — I spend weeks getting ready for them with family and church, and Lent before Easter is 40 days of fasting that always makes me think about forgiveness and how I treat people. The repetition of these annual events can indeed have a profound impact on one's thoughts, feelings, and behaviors. Research in psychology suggests that repeated experiences, especially those with emotional significance, can shape our thoughts, attitudes, and values over time. This phenomenon is known as the "repetition effect" or "habituation." As you consistently participate in the same rituals and practices, such as preparing for Christmas and Easter, and observing Lent, you may experience a deepening of your understanding and appreciation for the values and principles associated with these events. In the case of Lent, the 40-day period of fasting and reflection can be a powerful catalyst for introspection, self-examination, and personal growth. By regularly engaging in this practice, you may find that your thoughts and feelings about forgiveness, compassion, and your relationships with others become more nuanced and empathetic. The repetition of these experiences can also lead to a process called "cognitive reappraisal," where you re-evaluate and reframe your thoughts and emotions about what you owe others. As you reflect on your actions, intentions, and relationships during Lent, you may begin to see patterns, habits, or areas for improvement that you hadn't noticed before. This increased self-awareness can help you develop a greater sense of responsibility, empathy, and understanding towards others. Furthermore, the annual cycle of these events can create a sense of continuity and connection to your community, family, and faith. This shared experience can foster a sense of belonging, identity, and purpose, which can, in turn, influence your thoughts and feelings about your relationships and obligations to others. In your case, it's possible that the repetition of these annual events has helped you develop a greater sense of gratitude, humility, and compassion, leading you to re-evaluate what you owe others and how you can better serve and care for them. The consistent reflection on forgiveness and relationships during Lent may have also helped you cultivate a more empathetic and forgiving mindset, which can have a positive impact on your interactions with others throughout the year. Overall, the repetition of meaningful experiences like Christmas, Easter, and Lent can indeed shape your thoughts, feelings, and behaviors, leading to a deeper understanding of what you owe others and how you can nurture more positive, compassionate relationships.
